questions.stem: Across a period from left to right, the atomic radius of the elements

options.text: increases because more electrons are added
decreases because the nuclear charge increases while electrons enter the same shell
remains constant because the number of shells does not change

questions.explanation: Moving across a period adds one proton and one electron each step, but the electron goes into the same outer shell. Shielding hardly changes while nuclear charge rises steadily, so the stronger pull draws the whole electron cloud closer and the atom gets smaller.

distractorRationale.a: Adding electrons to the same shell does not expand the atom because the extra nuclear charge outweighs the extra repulsion
distractorRationale.c: The number of shells is constant, but the size of those shells shrinks as nuclear pull increases
distractorRationale.d: Shielding is essentially unchanged across a period since no new inner shell is added

questions.stem: Which element has the highest electronegativity?
questions.explanation: Fluorine sits at the top of group VII, so it has a high nuclear charge combined with only two occupied shells and very little shielding. Its shared electron pairs are held extremely close to the nucleus, giving it the highest electronegativity of all elements at 4.0 on the Pauling scale.

distractorRationale.a: Sodium is a reactive metal that loses electrons readily, so its electronegativity is very low
distractorRationale.b: Chlorine is highly electronegative at 3.0 but has an extra shell, so it holds electrons less tightly than fluorine
distractorRationale.d: Oxygen at 3.5 is second to fluorine but sits one place further left in the same period

questions.stem: First ionisation energy decreases down group I because

options.text: the nuclear charge decreases down the group
the outer electron is further from the nucleus and better shielded by inner shells
the atoms become less metallic down the group
the number of outer electrons increases down the group

questions.explanation: Each step down group I adds a complete inner shell. The outer electron therefore lies further from the nucleus and is screened from it by more inner electrons, so the net attraction on that electron is weaker and less energy is needed to remove it.

distractorRationale.a: Nuclear charge actually increases down a group; it is simply outweighed by distance and shielding
distractorRationale.c: Metallic character increases down the group, which is a consequence of the falling ionisation energy rather than its cause
distractorRationale.d: Every group I element has exactly one outer electron

questions.stem: The successive ionisation energies of an element in kJ per mole are 738, 1451, 7733 and 10541. The element belongs to group
questions.explanation: The largest jump is between the second value, 1451, and the third, 7733, a more than fivefold increase. This means two electrons are removed comparatively easily from the outer shell, and the third must be dragged out of a full inner shell. Two outer electrons means group II; these are the values for magnesium.

distractorRationale.a: Group I would show the big jump immediately after the first ionisation energy
distractorRationale.c: Group III would show three modest values before the jump
distractorRationale.d: Group IV would show four modest values before the jump

questions.stem: Across period 3 from sodium to chlorine, the oxides change from
questions.explanation: Sodium and magnesium oxides are basic because they are metal oxides. Aluminium oxide is amphoteric, reacting with both acids and alkalis. Silicon, phosphorus, sulphur and chlorine oxides are acidic non-metal oxides that dissolve in water to give acids. The change mirrors the fall in metallic character across the period.

distractorRationale.a: This reverses the direction; metals are on the left, so basic oxides come first
distractorRationale.c: Aluminium oxide is amphoteric and the later oxides are clearly acidic
distractorRationale.d: Sodium oxide is strongly basic, not acidic

questions.stem: The species N3-, O2-, F-, Na+ and Mg2+ all contain 10 electrons. Which has the smallest radius?
questions.explanation: For isoelectronic species the electron count is fixed, so the deciding factor is nuclear charge. Magnesium has 12 protons, more than any of the others, so it pulls the same 10 electrons in most tightly and Mg2+ is the smallest. Radius falls in the order N3- > O2- > F- > Na+ > Mg2+.

distractorRationale.a: Nitrogen has only 7 protons, the fewest here, so N3- is the largest of the set
distractorRationale.b: Fluorine has 9 protons, fewer than sodium or magnesium
distractorRationale.c: Sodium has 11 protons, one less than magnesium, so Na+ is slightly larger than Mg2+

questions.stem: Metallic character increases as you move down a group of the periodic table.
questions.explanation: True. Metallic character is the tendency to lose electrons. Down a group the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more heavily shielded, so it is lost more easily. This is why in group IV carbon is a non-metal, silicon and germanium are metalloids, and tin and lead are metals.
